Thepurposeofthisstudyistoexamineandcomparetheeffectofresidents’different
dimensions of place attachment on their word-of-mouth (WOM) behavior in two
cities: Sydney, Australia and Shanghai, China. A six-dimensional construct of place
attachment is proposed based upon a detailed literature review: four attitudinal
dimensions (place identity, place dependence, affective attachment, social bonding)
andtwo interactional dimensions(place memory,place expectation)are proposed to
reflect different aspects of a resident’s attachment to a place. To test the
dimensionalityofplaceattachmentandrelationshipsbetweenconstructs,asurveywas
completedby691residentsinthetwotargetedcities(361fromSydneyand330from
Shanghai),andastructuralequationmodelinginstrumentwasappliedtoanalyzethe
data. The findings of the empirical study statistically support the dimensionality of
place attachment proposed, and reveal that, in general, interactional dimensions of
place attachment have an effect on WOM behavior. The results suggest that WOM
behaviorofresidentsofthetwocitiesisinfluencedbydifferentattitudinaldimensions
of place attachment: Shanghai resident’s place identity and social bonding predict
one-to-oneWOM,whileSydneyresidents’affectiveattachmenttoSydneyinfluences
their one-to-one WOM behavior. This analysis provides insights into residents’
psychologyandbehaviorindifferenttourismdestinations,aswellasimportantinputs
for the sustainable development of destination branding and C2C tourism
communicationinthesetwocities.
Keywords: place attachment; destination branding; word-of-mouth; Sydney; Shang-
hai;structuralequationmodeling
Introduction
Developments in information and communication technology allow residents to play an
increasingly important role in tourism marketing and in attracting potential tourists to a
destination. This study investigates the motivation of local residents of a destination to
generate positive word of mouth (WOM) towards it. It is hypothesized that the
‘human(cid:1)placerelationship’,whichistherelationshipbetweenpeopleandplacesorspa-
tialsettings,isattheheartofunderstandingthisbehavior.
Residentsofadestinationare(oratleastassumedtobe)experiencedconsumerswho
benefitfromtourismthroughtheincomeandemploymentgeneratedbytheindustryorby
utilizing services and facilities at the destination that have been developed for tourism
(Choo, Park, & Petrick, 2011). Not surprisingly, a substantial volume of research

andaplace,orresidents’actualbehavioralinfluencesonadestination.ResearchbyEasterl-

ofthedestination,andthecharacteroflocalresidentsisonesymbolicattributeofthedesti-

in a destination’s positioning. Furthermore, destination brands and images are created by
Destination Management Organizations (DMOs) and destination stakeholders jointly, and
destination stakeholders’ performance can largely influence tourists’ interpretation of the
destination(Wagner,Peters,&Schuckert,2009).
Thisstudyaimstounderstandhowresidentsrecognize,understand,andidentifywith
their place (Choo, Park, & Petrick, 2011), and how their voluntary electronic WOM
behavior,promotingtheplaceasadestination,ismotivatedandgenerated.Tosetupthe
studycontext,aliteraturereviewonplaceattachment,WOManditsmotivationarepro-
vided.Hypothesesaredevelopedbasedontheconceptualizationofplaceattachmentand
WOM. Subsequently, the empirical study is described, including the research methodol-
ogy, and a description of the questionnaire and sample design. Finally, the findings are
presented and the relevant theoretical and managerial implications are discussed, with
suggestionsforfurtherresearch.
Literaturereview
Word-of-mouthande-Word-of-Mouth(orwordofmouse)
WOMhasbeenresearchedinthecontextofmarketingsince1960s(Arndt,1967;Dichter,
1966;Engel,Kegerreis,&Blackwell,1969).ThedefinitionsofWOMhaveevolvedover
time. In the early years, WOM was defined as “face-to-face communication about prod-
uctsorcompaniesbetweenthosepeoplewhowerenotcommercialentities”(Arndt,1967
citedinCarl,2006).Later,Westbrook(1987,p.261)definedWOMas“allinformalcom-
municationsdirectedatotherconsumersabouttheownership,usage,orcharacteristicsof
particulargoodsandservicesortheirsellers”.Withthespreadofelectronictechnologies,
WOMfurtherincludesvirtualinteractionsamongconsumers(Goldsmith,2006),whichis
usuallydenotedaseWordofMouth(eWOM)orwordofmouse.Followingtheevolution
ofthedefinitionsofWOM,theconsensusisthat“WOMisacommunicationopposedto
those through mass-media channels that pass product knowledge from producers/pro-
viders to consumers” (Litvin, Goldsmith, & Pan, 2008, p. 459). Thus, the key defining
characteristic ofWOMis the perceived independence ofthe source of the message. The
study follows Litvin et al. (2008, p. 459), who define WOM as “the communication
betweenconsumersaboutaproduct,service,oracompanyinwhichthesourcesarecon-
sideredindependentofcommercialinfluence”.

Tourism marketers have identified several reasons underpinning the critical impor-
tance of WOM. First,tourism product offerings often take the form of intangible goods,
whichcannotbeevaluatedbeforetheirconsumption,whileinterpersonalinfluences(usu-
ally based on WOM) can be a means of evaluating these offerings (Lewis & Chambers,
2000). Second, tourism products are often seen as a high-risk purchase, for which the
emotionalriskofreferencegroupevaluationisanimportantaspectofthedecision-mak-
ing process (Lewis & Chambers, 2000). Third, tourism products are both seasonal and
perishable, raising marketing stress levels for providers (Rao & Singhapakdi, 1997).
Fourth, since the tourism industry is intensely competitive in its products and services,
theuseofWOMmayprovideimportantcompetitiveadvantagesforearlyadopters(Litvin
etal.,2008).Consideringthedearthofhospitalityandtourismindustry-specificliterature
related to the issue, it would appear that the industry lags behind others in the develop-
mentanddiscussionofstrategiesformanagingWOM.
MotivationsofWOM/eWOM
One-to-oneWOMinthisstudyreferstothatgeneratedbyonepersonandcommunicated
toanotherpersonorasmallgroupofpeopleinprivate,suchasWOMthroughconversa-
tion with family or friends via emails, instant messaging, telephone, etc. This contrasts
with two other types of WOM behavior. Many-to-many and one-to-many WOMs relate
to situations where residents may use Web 2.0 social media websites such as Facebook
and Twitter, as well as online communities such as TripAdvisor to influence a tourist’s
destinationchoice(Tussyadiah&Fesenmaier,2009;Xiang&Gretzel,2010).One-to-one
WOM remains the keychannelandinformation source uponwhich anindividual poten-
tial tourist selects destinations. This paper will therefore focus on the associations
betweenplaceattachmentandone-to-oneWOM.
A group of motivations for WOM has been identified from previous studies. For
instance,Anderson(1998)suggeststhedisconfirmationofconsumption-relatedexpectations
may motivate WOM communication; Sundaram, Mitra, and Webster (1998) stress that
there is a difference in motivating positive WOM and negative WOM. Other motivations
have also been identified including involvement (Dichter, 1966), altruism (Sundaram et al.,
1998), self-enhancement (Engel, Blackwell, & Miniard, 1993), etc. Hennig-Thurau, Gwin-
ner,Walsh,andGremler(2004)provideasummaryofdifferentmotivesofWOM.
Mostofthesemotiveshavebeentestedinothercontexts.Hennig-Thurauetal.(2004)
findthatmotivesofeWOMincludingconsumers’desireforsocialinteraction,desirefor
economicincentives,concernforotherconsumers,andthepotentialtoenhancetheirown
self-wortharetheprimaryfactorsleadingtoeWOMbehavior.However,researchonthe
motivations of WOM is still focused on identifying the different motivations of WOM
andeWOM,insteadofidentifyingthedifferencesbetweenmotivationsofdifferenttypes
ofWOM,i.e.,one-to-oneWOM,one-to-manyWOM,andmany-to-manyWOM.
The applications of these findings to tourism have not been validated, while empirical
examples suggest the discussion on the motivation of residents in generating positive WOM
fortheirresidentdestinationmaybemorecomplex.Inaddition,littleresearchonthepossible
link between residents’ satisfaction of, or attachment to, their resident destination and their
positive WOM/eWOM about this destination, Choo, Park, & Petrick (2011) suggest place
attachment can directly influence the generation of WOM. Therefore, a review of the litera-
ture on the relationship between an individual and a place in order to examine the link
betweenthisrelationshipandresidentsdestinationpromotionrelevantbehaviorsisnecessary.

Placeattachment
Theconceptofplaceattachmentisrootedinattachmenttheory,influencedbyFreudand
other psychoanalytic thinkers. Bowlby formulated the basic tenets of the theory, while
Ainsworth’sinnovativemethodologymadeitpossibletotestBowlby’sideasempirically
identifying directions for further research (Ainsworth & Bowlby, 1991; Bremerton,
1992). Attachment has been defined as an affectional bond or tie between an individual
andanattachmentfigure,whichisabasichumanneedforsecurity(Bowlby,1969,1973,
1980).Moreover,Bremerton(1992)proposesthe“attachmentbehavioralsystem”,which
referstoapsychologicalorganizationhypothesizedtoexistwithinapersonthatregulates
behaviors designed to maintain or obtain proximity to and contact with the attachment
figure. For instance, a baby tends to develop behaviors which present its reliance on its
mother (attachment figure). This point of view of “attachment behavioral system” vali-
datesthecausalrelationshipbetweenattachmentandaseriesofrelevantbehaviors.
Beyond adolescent studies, the concept of attachmenthas been introduced into other
contexts to depict different bonding including person-to-person, and person-to-entity
such as an object or a place or an organization or a group. Concerning the attachment
betweenindividualsandplaces,avarietyofdisciplineshaveshownaninterestinunder-
standing the attachments that people form with places. Thus sociology emphasizes how
the symbolic meanings of place influence human interactions (Greider & Garkovich,
1994);environmentalpsychologydevelopstheconstructofplaceattachment(Altman&
Low,1992),whichrefersto“apositiveconnectionorbondbetweenapersonandapartic-
ular place” (Williams & Vaske, 2003). In environmental psychology, a number of
researchers apply themselves to conceptualize, understand, and measure attachment to
interpret the individual-individual, individual-community, and individual-place bonding
(Hay, 1998;Hidalgo &Hern(cid:1)andez,2001;Jorgensen &Stedman,2001;Kyle,Absher, &
Graefe,2003;Kyle,Bricker,Graefe,&Wickham,2004;Kyle,Graefe,&Manning,2005;
Kyle,Graefe,Manning,&Bacon,2004).
Recent research on place attachment considers the human(cid:1)place bond in terms of two
dimensions: place identity and place dependence, and this dimensionality is widely
accepted in the research fields of both environmental psychology and tourism management
(Kyle et al., 2005; Williams & Vaske, 2003; Yuksel, Yuksel, & Bilim, 2010). Other
researchers developed the place attachment model to include three, four, and even five
dimensions(Hammitt,Kyle,&Oh,,2009;Hammitt,Backlund,&Bixler,2004,2006).
Previous research has considered place attachment to be an outcome of the evaluation of
a place or one’s attitude toward this place, ignoring the fact that memorable or life-changing
eventscan also lead to an attachmentto aplace. Therefore in thisstudy, another two dimen-
sions of place attachment in terms of how an individual interacts with a place are included:
place memory indicates the memories of interactions associated with a place, while place
expectation is defined as one’s expectation of the future experiences perceived as likely to
occur in a place. With these two dimensions, the discussion of place attachment can be
extended to study the relationship between a tourist and a destination, since the interactions
in the tourism context do not have to relate to a long-term stay. In addition, the experience
thatone tourist has had in adestinationcancontribute the formation ofthe image of a desti-
nation(Moscardo,2010;Tung&Ritchie,2011).Sometouriststendtogobacktosomedesti-
nations again and again to re-trigger interactions in terms of their unforgettable experiences.
Chen,Dwyer,andFirth(2012)proposedasix-dimensionalconceptualizationofplaceattach-
ment, including both evaluations based and interactions based dimensions. This dimensional-
ityisappliedinthisstudytoexaminetheimpactofplaceattachmentondifferentbehaviors.

This assumption of relationship influencing WOM behavior has been tested in many
other contexts and subjects. In the employer(cid:1)employee context, it has been found that
identificationwithanorganizationhasanimpactonstaffretention(Bergami&Bagozzi,
2000;Dutton,Dukerich,&Harquail,1994).Harrison-Walker(2001)foundthatcommit-
menthasapositiveimpactonWOMactivities.Ahearne,Bhattacharya,andGruen(2005)
concluded that the stronger is the identification with the company, the stronger are the
customer in-role behaviors supportive of the company. Feather and Rauter (2004) found
thatorganizationalcitizenshipbehaviorsarepositivelyrelatedtoorganizationalcommit-
ment and organizational identification. Bettencourt (1997) found that there is a causal
relationship between a customer’s commitment to an organization and their voluntary
participationtoactivitieswhichcanimprovegovernanceanddevelopmentoftheorgani-
zation.BurmannandZeplin(2005),fromtheinternalbrandingperspective,definebrand
commitment as the extent of psychological attachment of employees to the brand and
arguedthatbrandcommitmentcaninfluenceemployees’intentiontoexertbrandcitizen-
ship behavior. These findings from different contexts validate the relationship between
residents’ place attachment and their positive WOM behavior which can help promote
theirplaceasadestination.
Previousresearchhasfoundseveralpredictorsofone-to-oneWOM.Theseincludethe
following:concernfor others (a genuine desire tohelp a friend or relative make abetter
purchase decision), message intrigue (entertainment resulting from talking about certain
adsorsellingappeals)(Engeletal.,1993;Sundarametal.,1998),andadesiretohelpthe
place (Sundaram et al., 1998). In other words, residents may talk about their resident
placetorelativesorfriendsastourismrecommendations,ortalkaboutinterestingactivi-
ties or events in the past or the future, or merely have the desire to help the place.

Therefore, residents’ place memory and place expectation may have an impact on their
one-to-oneWOMintention.
Hencethesecondhypothesisisasfollows:
H2:Themoreattachedresidentsaretotheplace,themoretheygenerateone-to-oneWOM.
A model based on the nature, antecedents, and consequences of the construct of
place attachment is proposed to explore the mechanisms by which place attachment
may influence residents’ WOM behavior topromote the place asa destination. The pro-
posed model identifies two main phases in the formation of residents’ attachment to the
place and their WOM behavior toward the place: (1) residents’ internalization process
and (2) residents’ output process (Figure 1). In the internalization process, residents
automatically transfer their evaluation and interaction of their resident place into their
attachment to it. In the output process, residents voluntarily generated their WOM
behavior to assist in promoting the place as a tourism destination, sometimes con-
sciously,butmostly subconsciously.

Researchmethodology
A survey approach was employed to test the hypotheses. Data were collected from resi-
dentsoftwocities:ShanghaiandSydney.Mostoftheitemsselectedinthequestionnaire
arefrompastresearchwhichhasbeenshownabletobereliablyappliedtoadifferentcon-
text.Theitemsofthetwointeraction-baseddimensions ofplace attachment were devel-
oped prior this research following the approach to scale development proposed by
DeVellis(2003).ToensuretheintegratedquestionnaireitemswererelevanttoShanghai
andSydneyresidents,theauthorsdiscussedwhatwouldbemostappropriateforthisstudy
withanexpertpanelincludingscholars,travelagents,tourists,andShanghaiandSydney
residents. A small pilot study was conducted to clarify the coverage of the constructs
includedinthisstudy.
Samplinganddatacollectionprocedures
This study used a stratified sample of 330 Shanghai residents and 361 Sydney residents
who have lived in Shanghai or Sydney for at least one year. An online survey was
designedandappliedtocollectdata,andthepostcodewasrecordedinthesurveytoindi-
catethedifferentdistrictsinwhichtherespondentsliveforbothSydneyandShanghai.A
quotawasdeterminedforeachpostcodeintheonlinesurveytomakesurethedistribution
inthesampleismainlylocatedinthecenterofthecityandbasicallyconsistentwiththe
distribution in the demographic statistics. The survey was conducted from November
2011 through March 2012. The demographic profile information of the respondents is
listedinTable1.ThedistributionofsamplesisillustratedinthemapsofFigures2and3.
Measurement
Themeasurementofone-to-oneWOMisappliedfromdifferentempiricalstudiesindif-
ferent research realms. Previous research on WOM has used a single-item Likert-type
scale to assess WOM (Danaher & Rust, 1996; Singh, 1990; Swan & Oliver, 1989).
Another main stream of research on WOM measures the intention of WOM instead of
actualaction(Danaher&Rust,1996).
Arnett,German,andHunt(2003)developedathree-itemscaletoexaminethegeneral
WOM.ThismeasurewasappliedbyMorhart,Herzog,andTomczak(2009).Inthepres-
entstudy,thismeasurewasappliedtotestone-to-oneWOMbehaviorofaresidentfora
destination. A three-item, 7-point Likert scale to measure the overall place satisfaction
was applied in this study. The responding residents were asked to evaluate their overall
satisfactionwiththeirresidentplaceindicating1as‘Verydissatisfied’and7as‘Verysat-
isfied’. The measure of evaluation- and attitude-based place attachment has been widely
used in relevant studies. Fifteen items summarized from previous studies were adapted
including Yuksel et al.’s (2009), Nielsen-Pincus, Hall, Force, and Wulfhorst’s (2010),
andKyleetal.’s(2005)placeattachmentscale.
Dataanalysisandresults
DatawereanalyzedusingIBMSPSSstatistics20andIBMSPSSAmos20software.Con-
firmatoryfactor analysis (CFA) was conducted totest the validity of the indicator varia-
bles. Structural equation modeling (SEM) was thereafter used to identify relationships
amongtheconstructsinthehypotheses.

Discussionandimplications
In this study, one-to-one WOMs were considered dependent variables, respectively, and
the mediating effects of place attachment between satisfaction and one-to-one WOM
were found to be statistically significant. For the residents’ internalization process, the
results illustrate a strong positive and direct relationship between satisfaction of a place
andthedifferentdimensionsoftheevaluationbasedattachmenttothisplace(Hypothesis
group 1). The results are consistent with previous research (Lee, Kyle, & Scott, 2012;
Prayag&Ryan,2012).Inaddition,strongcorrelationswerefoundamongplacesatisfac-
tion, place memory, and place expectation. The findings indicate that place satisfaction
remains a key factor which can influence how a resident forms the relationship with the
place, andsuggesturbanstakeholdersofSydneyandShanghaishouldproactivelyinvest
moreinimprovinginfrastructure,accessibility,andservicelevelstoachieveahighersat-
isfaction level of the residents, if they aim to leverage the relationship between the resi-
dentsandtheirresidentcities.ThisisextremelyimportantforimmigrantcitiesasSydney
and Shanghai, since place satisfaction is identified as an important antecedent of place
attachmentandhasasignificantinfluenceontheevaluationandcomparisonbetweendif-
ferentplacesofresidence(Chen,Dwyer,&Firth,2014).
